passage: Siddiq had heard it at least six times that week in the office kitchen in Cape Town: the number 12 bus route was being scrapped at the end of the month. Thabo had said it. The receptionist had said it. Someone had pinned a sad note about it on the board. Siddiq was halfway through an email to his team suggesting they move their meeting times when he stopped, fingers above the keys. Have I actually checked this, he wondered, or have I just heard it a lot? He opened the transport department's own notices page. The route wasn't being scrapped. It was being moved two streets over for three weeks of road repairs. He deleted the email and walked to the kitchen. "Thabo, the 12 isn't going anywhere. Just a detour." Thabo frowned. "But everyone said..." "I know. I believed it too, because everyone said it."

qa.q: What was really happening to the number 12 route?
qa.a: It was being moved two streets over for three weeks of road repairs.

qa.q: What made Siddiq stop in the middle of the email?
qa.a: Siddiq wondered whether the claim had actually been checked or only heard many times, and that doubt was enough to pause.

qa.q: Which step turned the rumour into something Siddiq could rely on?
qa.a: Opening the transport department's own notices page, one first-hand source, instead of counting how many people had said it.

qa.q: How might Thabo feel when Siddiq brings the news?
qa.a: Thabo is surprised and a little defensive, but Siddiq admitting to believing it too makes it easier for Thabo to accept.

grounding: A young man asks whether he has checked a rumour or only heard it often, reads the official notice, and admits he had believed it too.

passage: Preeti was making slides in the school staffroom for Saturday's parent workshop when she typed it: "Every child has a learning style: visual, listening or hands-on. Teach to it!" She had heard that line at every training since college, on posters, and from Vijay across the table only yesterday. She looked at it, then typed a small note in the margin: Checked, or just heard a lot? Honestly, just heard. At lunch she read one long review by education researchers, the original, not a summary. It said matching lessons to a child's preferred style hadn't shown the gains people claimed, and that mixing ways of teaching helped everyone. She deleted the slide. "Vijay," she said, "you know the learning styles thing? I've repeated it for years. Turns out familiar isn't the same as true." Vijay put his tea down. "Show me."

qa.q: What note did Preeti type in the margin?
qa.a: Checked, or just heard a lot?

qa.q: What was Preeti realising when she answered her own note with "Honestly, just heard"?
qa.a: She was realising, a little uncomfortably, that the line felt true only because she had met it at every training, on posters and from Vijay, not because she had ever checked it.

qa.q: Why was reading the original review a better choice than asking around the staffroom?
qa.a: Asking around would only bring back the same repeated claim, while one first-hand source showed what had actually been found.

qa.q: How might the parents at Saturday's workshop be affected by Preeti's choice?
qa.a: They will hear a better-grounded message and won't go home trying to sort their children into styles the research did not support.

grounding: A teacher questions a familiar claim before a workshop, reads one original review, and admits familiarity had stood in for checking.

passage:
Dear Zubin,
You forwarded the "free metro on Sundays from next month" message to the family group this morning, and I nearly replied "Finally!" I'd heard it from Masi, from two colleagues and from our building guard. It felt settled.
Then I asked myself something I'm trying to make a habit: have I checked this, or have I just heard it a lot? Just heard it, honestly. So I went to the metro corporation's own website and read their notices. Nothing about free Sundays. There's a discount for students, that's all.
I'm not writing to scold you. I nearly shared it myself, and the only reason it felt true was that it was everywhere. Could you post a short correction in the group? Masi listens to you more than to me.
Love,
Ritu

qa.q: What did Ritu find on the metro corporation's website?
qa.a: Nothing about free Sundays, only a discount for students.

qa.q: Why did the free-metro claim feel settled to Ritu at first?
qa.a: Ritu had heard it from Masi, two colleagues and the building guard, so it felt true simply because it was everywhere.

qa.q: What does Ritu ask Zubin to do, and why is that a good next step?
qa.a: Post a short correction in the family group, since Masi listens to Zubin more, which can stop the rumour spreading.

qa.q: How might Zubin feel reading the email?
qa.a: Zubin might feel a little embarrassed, but Ritu admitting to nearly sharing it too makes the correction feel friendly rather than like a scolding. 🙂

grounding: A young adult asks whether a claim was checked or just heard often, reads the official source, and admits it only felt true from repetition.

passage: So, Lalit, you asked why I didn't sign the petition. Here's Chaitanya's slightly embarrassing answer. For a month I'd heard that the old municipal library near our college was being knocked down for a mall. Heard it from the chai stall, from two colleagues, from my mother's building group. I believed it completely. I even started a sad post about it. Then I stopped and asked myself: have I actually checked this, or have I just heard it a lot? Just heard it. Every single time. So I went to the corporation's website and found the ward's works notice. It wasn't demolition. It was repairs to the roof, three months, then it reopens. I sat there feeling a bit foolish. The claim felt true because it was familiar, and familiar told me nothing. I deleted my post and sent the notice to the chai stall uncle.

qa.q: What did the corporation's works notice actually say about the library?
qa.a: It said the library was getting roof repairs for three months and would then reopen.

qa.q: Why did Chaitanya feel a bit foolish after reading the notice?
qa.a: Because the claim had felt completely true, though it had only ever been heard, never checked.

qa.q: What habit helped Chaitanya most here, and why?
qa.a: Asking "have I checked this, or just heard it a lot?" and then going to the primary source, the ward's works notice, instead of relying on repetition.

qa.q: How might the chai stall uncle react to getting the notice?
qa.a: The uncle might be surprised and relieved, and perhaps pass the real news on to the stall's customers instead of the rumour.

grounding: An adult asks whether a claim is checked or just familiar, reads the primary source, and admits familiarity proved nothing.

passage: I'm Gopika, and I sit opposite Sangeeta at the design agency. For two weeks everyone on our floor had been saying the office would switch to a four-day week from April. You heard it at the coffee machine, in the lift, in the lunch queue. Last Tuesday, someone asked Sangeeta about it and she started to nod, then stopped. She said, "Actually, I've heard that maybe twenty times, but I've never read it anywhere." Then she opened the staff portal and searched for the HR circular. She read it out to our row: the four-day week was a pilot, for one small team, for one month. She laughed and said, "I'd have sworn it was for all of us. Hearing it a lot doesn't make it so." I don't know if she was annoyed, but she sent the link to our group straight away.

qa.q: What did the HR circular actually say about the four-day week?
qa.a: It was a pilot for one small team, for one month.

qa.q: What does Sangeeta's stopping mid-nod suggest she realised?
qa.a: She seemed surprised and a little doubtful, noticing she had heard the claim many times but never checked it, so her certainty wasn't based on anything.

qa.q: Which step in Sangeeta's approach could anyone copy, and why does it work?
qa.a: Opening the actual HR circular, the primary source, settles the question in a minute instead of relying on how often a claim is repeated.

qa.q: How might the colleagues in the group feel when they get the link?
qa.a: Some might feel disappointed about the four-day week, but most would probably be glad to know the real plan before making any arrangements.

grounding: A colleague watches an adult separate heard-often from checked by reading the primary source and admitting her error.
